clue.text: See 15
Eliza was mistaken for one of them.

definitions.text: Eliza was mistaken for one of them.

parts.words: Eliza was mistaken for one of them
parts.note: in My Fair Lady, the phonetics expert Zoltan Karpathy declares at the ball that Eliza Doolittle is of Magyar royal blood

explanation.walkthrough: Eliza is Eliza Doolittle of Pygmalion and My Fair Lady. At the embassy ball the rival linguist Karpathy announces that she must be a Hungarian princess.
explanation.definitionFit: The nationality the impostor-spotter at the ball assigned to the flower girl, in the plural because she is 'one of them'.

clue.text: Is the USSR set to produce such supports?

indicators.note: the letters of USSR and set are worked into something new, as raw material is used to produce goods

explanation.surface: A Cold War question: is the Soviet Union ready to manufacture some kind of structural props?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' looks like the verb meaning ready, but it is part of the letters: 'to produce' tells you to rework USSR plus SET into a new word.
explanation.definitionFit: Trusses are frameworks of beams that hold up a roof or bridge, a kind of support.

clue.text: When someone quotes like this, zeros would appropriately be involved.

definitions.text: When someone quotes like this, zeros would appropriately be involved.

parts.words: When someone quotes like this, zeros would appropriately be involved
parts.note: quoting approximate numbers that end in noughts, and a zero is itself a circular digit

explanation.walkthrough: Quoting a figure approximately means rounding it, which leaves trailing zeros; the joke is that a zero is literally a round figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means approximately, rounded off to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand.

clue.text: Leaning? Learn it the hard way!

indicators.note: learning something the hard way suggests struggling and twisting it about, so the letters of learn it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Advice to someone inclined to depend on others: you'll have to discover independence through painful experience.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaning on someone means depending on them, which is the sense of the adjective for dependent.

clue.text: See 23
Certainly not found on a king of the Mercians!

parts.note: something that is off is not on at all

explanation.surface: An exclamation that something is definitely absent from an Anglo-Saxon monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Offa was an eighth-century king of Mercia, the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of the English Midlands, famous for the earthwork Offa's Dyke; the answer splits as OFF A, 'not on a'.
explanation.definitionFit: Offa ruled Mercia from 757 to 796, the most powerful English monarch of his era.

clue.text: In Africa, well-known miler of a sort — with a different movement.

indicators.note: the letters of miler of are sorted into a new order
the letters move about into a different arrangement, and movement also hints at the political sense

explanation.surface: A famous African middle-distance runner of some kind, but one with an unusual running action.
explanation.walkthrough: The miler looks like an athlete, but 'a sort' and 'with a different movement' both tell you to rearrange MILER OF. FRELIMO is the Mozambique Liberation Front, well known across Africa in the 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mozambican liberation movement won independence from Portugal in 1975 and was widely reported throughout the continent.

clue.text: See 12
Commonly objective, though Zola didn't confine his grammatical construction to it.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the accusative is the grammatical case commonly called the objective case

definitions.text: though Zola didn't confine his grammatical construction to it
definitions.meaning: second meaning: Zola's famous J'accuse letter made an accusation, a case that went well beyond grammar into the Dreyfus affair

explanation.walkthrough: Zola wrote J'accuse in defence of Dreyfus; the clue jokes that his 'accusative case' was a legal campaign, not only a grammatical one.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar the case of a direct object is called accusative, known in English grammar as the objective case.

clue.text: What one might be expected to start in, and yet run late, possibly.

definitions.text: What one might be expected to start in

indicators.note: signals that the letters of run late might possibly be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: Someone expected to set off promptly who may well still be running late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' tells you to rearrange RUN LATE. The definition refers to a car: you start the engine with the gearbox out of gear.
explanation.definitionFit: Drivers are expected to start the engine with the gear lever in the position where no gear is engaged.

clue.text: He was in the vanguard of many French movements.

definitions.text: He was in the vanguard of many French movements.

parts.words: He was in the vanguard of many French movements
parts.note: an avant-garde artist active in surrealism, cubist circles, ballet, film and poetry

explanation.walkthrough: Jean Cocteau, poet, playwright and film-maker, was a leading figure across several French artistic movements of the early twentieth century.
explanation.definitionFit: The French writer and artist moved through many avant-garde schools, which is what being in the vanguard means.

clue.text: Implies some pretty low eavesdropping would make a rather tight case.

definitions.text: Implies some pretty low eavesdropping would make a rather tight case.

parts.words: Implies some pretty low eavesdropping would make a rather tight case
parts.note: a bug is a listening device, and one hidden in a floor covering is very low down

explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the phrase is a bug (eavesdropping device) placed in a rug (low down); the idiom describes something snugly enclosed.
explanation.definitionFit: The simile means very cosy and comfortably wrapped up, like a tight-fitting case.

clue.text: Those who dislike chocolates perhaps can't, but they're superficially used by many women.

definitions.text: Those who dislike chocolates perhaps can't
definitions.meaning: first meaning: people who hate cream-filled chocolates can't ..., i.e. can't bear them

definitions.text: they're superficially used by many women
definitions.meaning: second meaning: cosmetic lotions applied to the surface of the skin

explanation.walkthrough: Creams are cream-filled chocolates, and 'face' means bear; split differently, the phrase names skin cosmetics.
explanation.definitionFit: Moisturising lotions are applied to the skin's surface, which is why the clue says superficially.

clue.text: What's July 4th? That's what many say when setting up a meeting.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Independence Day is a particular day on the calendar

definitions.text: That's what many say when setting up a meeting
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the phrase agreeing to an appointment

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is answered literally, since July 4th is a calendar day; the second is the stock phrase for confirming plans.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase confirms an arranged appointment, and literally states that something is a calendar day.

clue.text: One would hardly be 12-8, even in play.

definitions.text: One would hardly be 12-8, even in play.

parts.words: One would hardly be 12-8, even in play
parts.note: an animal on scorching metal would be anything but cosy, and the phrase is also the title of a stage drama

explanation.walkthrough: 12-8 is AS SNUG AS A BUG IN A RUG. Tennessee Williams's play takes its title from the image of a restless creature on burning metal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tennessee Williams play's title pictures a jittery animal, the opposite of cosy contentment.

clue.text: The big exhibition called off wasn't cricket.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: if the fair is cancelled there is ...
second meaning: an exclamation that something was unjust

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not cricket' is a British idiom for unsporting or unfair behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: The playground protest means that something was unjust or unsporting.

clue.text: Would one feel sheepish to be so taken in?

definitions.text: Would one feel sheepish to be so taken in?

parts.words: Would one feel sheepish to be so taken in
parts.note: being swindled leaves one embarrassed, and a sheep relieved of its wool has also been sheared

explanation.walkthrough: Sheepish means embarrassed, but it also points to sheep, whose wool coat is a fleece.
explanation.definitionFit: Being swindled or cheated is slang for being taken in, as a sheep loses its wool.

clue.text: Certain to be a print?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: in photography, the image with true tones made from a negative

explanation.walkthrough: The photographic sense is the opposite of a negative.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means sure, and in photography names the image printed from a negative.

clue.text: With the road not torn up, such things stink!

definitions.note: the definition describes the answer as a smelly substance, a singular noun

indicators.note: a road that is torn up is dug apart, so the letters of road and not are broken and reassembled

explanation.surface: A grumble that roads left undisturbed somehow still smell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not torn up' reads as a road left intact, but 'torn up' acts on ROAD plus NOT together.
explanation.definitionFit: A substance that gives off a smell, used for example to scent gas so leaks can be detected.

clue.text: Unionized three before 25?

parts.note: the state that joined the Union three admissions ahead of the state at 25-across

explanation.walkthrough: 25-across is ALABAMA, admitted as the 22nd state in 1819; Indiana was the 19th, in 1816. Unionized looks like trade unions but means joined the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiana entered the Union as the nineteenth state, three admissions before Alabama.

clue.text: He composed the changing scene, and nothing more.

indicators.note: a scene change in theatre moves things about, so the letters of scene are rearranged

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A theatre composer wrote the music for the scene change and nothing more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing' tells you to rearrange SCENE together with O for 'nothing'. George Enescu (Enesco) was a Romanian composer and violinist.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romanian violinist and composer wrote the Romanian Rhapsodies and the opera Oedipe.

clue.text: Possibly the sequel to "Address Unknown."

parts.note: Address Unknown is a title of a novel and film, but also the postal stamp for undeliverable mail

explanation.walkthrough: A letter marked 'address unknown' is sent back with the postal endorsement that follows; the clue pretends both are book or film titles.
explanation.definitionFit: The postal instruction for mail that cannot be delivered, which naturally follows an unknown address.

clue.text: Maybe Cassius' understanding — though his followers might trust he hasn't.

definitions.text: Maybe Cassius' understanding — though his followers might trust he hasn't.

parts.words: Maybe Cassius' understanding — though his followers might trust he hasn't
parts.note: understanding jokingly means what one stands on, and Cassius Clay was the boxer's birth name

explanation.walkthrough: Muhammad Ali was born Cassius Clay, so what he stands on would be his feet made of Clay; his fans would trust he has no hidden weakness, the idiom's meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means a hidden flaw or weakness in a person who is admired.

clue.text: Evidently avoids a problem of chess we devised.

indicators.note: a chess problem is a composed puzzle, signalling that the letters are worked over
the letters of chess we are devised, put together in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A chess problem we composed which conspicuously sidesteps something.
explanation.definitionFit: To eschew is to deliberately shun or abstain from something, which the solver sees evidently happening.

clue.text: A state, by the French educational standards.

parts.note: la is the feminine form of 'the' in French
BA and MA, the Bachelor and Master of Arts degrees

explanation.surface: Describing a nation's condition, as judged by France's school benchmarks.
explanation.definitionFit: Alabama is one of the fifty US states, in the Deep South.

clue.text: The Bay of Fundy should be neat!

definitions.text: The Bay of Fundy should be
definitions.meaning: first meaning, a pun: the bay has the world's highest tides, so it ought to be full of tides
second meaning: orderly and well kept

explanation.walkthrough: The Bay of Fundy, between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, has the world's largest tidal range; the clue plays on 'tide-y'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means neat and orderly, and its sound suggests full of tides.

clue.text: For openers, they shouldn't present a problem. (Pop's life may depend on them!)

definitions.text: For openers, they shouldn't present a problem. (Pop's life may depend on them!)

parts.words: For openers, they shouldn't present a problem. (Pop's life may depend on them!)
parts.note: pop is fizzy soda, which goes flat unless its container stays sealed by its lid

explanation.walkthrough: 'For openers' seems to mean 'to begin with', but it means bottle openers; Pop is not a father but soda.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal crimped lids seal soda bottles, keeping the fizz in, and an opener should lift them easily.
